title: Why Game-Based Learning Works for Children Aged 5–13
excerpt: Research shows that children learn up to 40% faster when content is delivered through play. Here's the science behind Sodafom's approach.

body.text: Game-based learning (GBL) isn't a new idea — educators have known for decades that children absorb information more effectively when they're engaged and having fun. But the research behind it has never been stronger.

A 2023 meta-analysis of over 200 studies found that students in game-based learning environments scored an average of 14 percentile points higher on assessments than those in traditional classroom settings. The key factor? Intrinsic motivation — children play because they want to, not because they have to.

At Sodafom, every game is built around a core learning objective tied to the UK National Curriculum. Number Pop teaches counting and number recognition. Spelling Bee builds phonological awareness. Reading Quest develops comprehension and inference skills. The game is the vehicle; the learning is the destination.

Age-adaptive difficulty is another critical piece. A 6-year-old and an 11-year-old have very different cognitive profiles. Our three-tier system — Ages 5–7, 8–10, and 11–13 — ensures every child is challenged at exactly the right level, keeping them in the 'flow state' where learning happens fastest.
The result? Children who ask to do their homework. Parents who see real progress. Teachers who have a tool that actually engages the whole class. That's the Sodafom promise.

title: 5 Ways to Support Your Child's Maths at Home (Ages 5–7)
excerpt: The early years of maths are all about building number sense. Here are five practical, fun activities you can do at home to give your child a head start.

body.text: Maths anxiety starts early — often before children even reach Key Stage 1. The good news is that a few minutes of playful maths each day can make a huge difference to your child's confidence and ability.
1. Count everything. Stairs, grapes, cars on the street. Counting out loud builds number sense naturally and costs nothing. Make it a game: 'Can you count the steps before I do?'
2. Play with shapes. Spot circles, squares, and triangles on your walk to school. Ask 'how many sides does that sign have?' Shape recognition is a core Year 1 objective and it's everywhere.
3. Use real money. Even plastic coins help children understand value and simple addition. Set up a pretend shop and let them be the shopkeeper.
4. Tell number stories. 'There were 5 birds on the fence. 2 flew away. How many are left?' Story problems build the mental model for subtraction without a worksheet in sight.

5. Play Sodafom's Number Pop. Our balloon-popping game targets exactly the counting and number recognition skills in the Year 1 and Year 2 curriculum — and children genuinely love it. Ten minutes before bed beats a maths worksheet every time.

title: How to Help Your Primary School Child Improve Their Spelling
excerpt: Spelling is one of the most common areas where children fall behind — but it's also one of the easiest to improve with the right approach at home.

body.text: Spelling is one of those skills that looks simple from the outside but is actually a complex blend of phonological awareness, visual memory, and morphological knowledge. When children struggle, it's rarely because they're not trying hard enough.

The most effective approach combines three things: hearing words (phonics), seeing words (visual patterns), and writing words (muscle memory). Traditional 'look, cover, write, check' works precisely because it hits all three.

But repetition alone isn't enough — children need to encounter words in context. Reading widely is the single biggest predictor of spelling ability. Children who read for pleasure for just 20 minutes a day encounter an estimated 1.8 million words per year.
For tricky words — the ones that don't follow phonics rules — mnemonics and word stories help. 'Because: Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants.' Silly, memorable, and it works.

Sodafom's Spelling Bee and Word Wizard games target the most common spelling patterns in the KS1 and KS2 curriculum. Children hear the word, see it, and type it — hitting all three learning channels in a format they actually want to use. Five minutes a day, three times a week, and most children see measurable improvement within a month.

title: Easy Science Experiments for Primary School Children (No Lab Required)
excerpt: You don't need a laboratory to spark a love of science. These five simple experiments use everyday household items and cover real KS1 and KS2 science objectives.

body.text: Science is the subject children are most curious about — and the one most likely to be squeezed out of the school day. The good news is that the best science happens at home, with things you already have.

1. Baking soda and vinegar volcano. Mix bicarbonate of soda with vinegar and watch the fizzing reaction. Ask your child: 'Is this a physical change or a chemical change?' (It's chemical — a new gas, carbon dioxide, is produced.) This covers KS2 chemistry: reversible and irreversible changes.

2. Celery and food colouring. Stand a stick of celery in a glass of water with a few drops of food colouring. Over 24 hours, the colour travels up the stem. This demonstrates how plants transport water — a core KS2 biology objective.

3. Shadow clocks. On a sunny day, place a stick in the ground and mark where its shadow falls every hour. By the end of the day, you've built a sundial and explored how the Earth's rotation affects light — KS2 Earth and Space.
4. Egg in a bottle. Heat a glass bottle, place a peeled hard-boiled egg on the opening, and watch it get sucked in as the air cools and contracts. Air pressure made visible — perfect for ages 10–13.

5. Reinforce it with Sodafom. Our Science games — Animal Kingdom Quiz, Nature Explorer, and Science Experiments — turn these concepts into interactive challenges. Children who do the experiment and then play the game retain the knowledge far longer than either activity alone.

title: How to Boost Reading Comprehension for Children Aged 8–13
excerpt: Reading the words is only half the battle. True comprehension — understanding, inferring, and evaluating — is a skill that needs to be taught. Here's how.

body.text: Many children who read fluently still struggle with comprehension. They can decode every word on the page but can't tell you what the passage was about, or why a character made a particular choice. This is one of the most common issues teachers flag at parents' evenings.

The gap between decoding and comprehension usually comes down to vocabulary and background knowledge. A child who doesn't know what 'reluctant' means will miss the emotional weight of a sentence. Building vocabulary through wide reading — fiction, non-fiction, comics, anything — is the single most effective intervention.

Ask questions while you read together. Not just 'what happened?' but 'why do you think she did that?' and 'what do you think will happen next?' These inference questions are exactly what SATs and GCSEs test, and they're best practised in a low-stakes, conversational setting.

Teach children to 'read between the lines'. Authors don't always say things directly — they show them. When a character 'slammed the door', the author is telling us something about their emotional state without using the word 'angry'. Spotting these clues is a skill that improves with practice.

Summarising is another powerful tool. After reading a chapter, ask your child to tell you what happened in three sentences. This forces them to identify the most important information — a skill that transfers directly to essay writing.

Sodafom's Reading Quest and Story Builder games are designed specifically to develop these comprehension skills. Children read short passages and answer inference, vocabulary, and evaluation questions — the same question types they'll face in Year 6 SATs and beyond.

title: Why 10 Minutes a Day Beats 2 Hours on Sunday
excerpt: The science of learning is clear: short, daily practice is dramatically more effective than long, infrequent sessions. Here's why — and how Sodafom's Daily Challenge is built around this principle.

body.text: Most parents intuitively feel that regular practice is better than cramming — but the science behind it is even more compelling than you might think. The phenomenon is called 'spaced repetition', and it's one of the most well-replicated findings in cognitive psychology.

When we learn something and then revisit it after a short gap, the act of retrieval strengthens the memory trace. Each time we retrieve a memory, it becomes more durable. This is why a child who practises times tables for 10 minutes every day for a week will outperform one who does 70 minutes in a single sitting — even though the total time is identical.

The 'forgetting curve', first described by Hermann Ebbinghaus in 1885, shows that we forget roughly 50% of new information within an hour, and 70% within 24 hours — unless we review it. Daily practice interrupts this curve at exactly the right moment.

Consistency also builds habit. A child who plays one Sodafom game every evening before dinner doesn't have to decide to do it — it just happens. Habits require no willpower, which is why they're so powerful for children (and adults).

This is exactly why we built the Daily Challenge. Every day, a new featured game is unlocked — and children who complete it earn 5 bonus stars. It's a small, achievable goal that keeps the habit alive and the learning consistent. Ten minutes a day, every day, is the most powerful educational investment a parent can make.

title: Do Badges and Rewards Actually Motivate Children to Learn?
excerpt: Gamification in education is sometimes dismissed as gimmicky — but the research tells a more nuanced story. Here's what the evidence says about using rewards to build learning habits.

body.text: The debate about extrinsic rewards in education has been going on for decades. One camp argues that rewards undermine intrinsic motivation — that children who are paid to read will stop reading when the payment stops. The other argues that rewards build habits that eventually become self-sustaining. Who's right?

The truth, as usual, is in the details. Research by Deci and Ryan (1985) found that tangible, expected rewards for activities children already enjoy can reduce intrinsic motivation. But rewards for activities children are neutral about — or initially resistant to — can build engagement that eventually becomes intrinsic.

The key is the type of reward. Informational rewards — those that give feedback about competence ('You've mastered 3-digit addition!') — consistently increase intrinsic motivation. Controlling rewards ('Do this to get that') are more likely to undermine it.

Sodafom's badge system is designed around informational rewards. Each of our 22 badges represents a genuine achievement — completing 10 games, earning 100 stars, mastering a subject. The badge tells the child something true about their ability. It's not a bribe; it's a milestone marker.

Stars work similarly. They're not given for showing up — they're earned based on performance (50%+ score for 1 star, 75%+ for 2, 90%+ for 3). This means they carry information: a 3-star score means something. Children quickly learn to aim for 3 stars not because of the stars themselves, but because they want to know they've truly mastered the material.

The goal of any reward system should be to make itself unnecessary. At Sodafom, we see children who start playing for the stars and badges, and end up playing because they genuinely love learning. That transition — from extrinsic to intrinsic motivation — is the real win.

title: Screen Time: When Is It Educational and When Is It Just Passive?
excerpt: Not all screen time is equal. Here's a practical guide for parents on how to tell the difference — and how to make the most of the time your child spends on a device.

body.text: The phrase 'screen time' has become a catch-all that lumps together watching cartoons, playing educational games, video-calling grandparents, and scrolling social media. These are not the same thing — and treating them as equivalent does children a disservice.

The American Academy of Pediatrics and the UK's Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health have both moved away from blanket time limits in favour of a more nuanced approach: what matters is the quality and context of screen use, not just the quantity.

Passive screen time — watching videos, scrolling feeds — activates the brain's reward system without requiring any cognitive effort. It's the digital equivalent of junk food: enjoyable in the moment, but not nourishing. The concern isn't the screen; it's the displacement of activities that build skills (reading, physical play, conversation).

Active screen time is different. When a child is solving a maths puzzle, building a story, or answering comprehension questions, they're doing cognitive work. The screen is a tool, not a destination. Research consistently shows that interactive, educational screen use has positive effects on literacy and numeracy — particularly for children aged 3–8.

Practical questions to ask: Does the activity require the child to think, respond, or create? Does it have a clear learning objective? Does it give feedback? Is there a natural stopping point? If the answer to most of these is yes, you're likely looking at educational screen time.

Sodafom games are designed to be active, not passive. Every game requires a response, gives immediate feedback, and has a clear end point. We also build in natural breaks — the game ends, the stars are awarded, and the child is encouraged to go do something else. Learning should be a sprint, not a marathon.

title: Times Tables: The Most Effective Ways to Help Your Child Master Them
excerpt: Times tables are the foundation of almost all secondary school maths. Here's what actually works — and what doesn't — based on the latest research.

body.text: The Multiplication Tables Check (MTC) in Year 4 has focused minds on times tables in a way that hasn't been seen since the days of rote chanting. Children are now expected to recall any multiplication fact up to 12×12 in under 6 seconds. That's a high bar — and it requires a specific kind of practice.

The bad news: passive exposure doesn't work. Listening to a times tables song in the car is better than nothing, but it won't produce the rapid, automatic recall the MTC requires. That needs active retrieval practice — being asked a question and having to produce the answer.

The good news: it doesn't take long. Research by the Education Endowment Foundation suggests that 10 minutes of daily retrieval practice over 6 weeks is enough for most children to achieve fluency across all tables. The key word is daily — see our article on spaced repetition for why consistency matters so much.

Start with the easy ones. 2s, 5s, and 10s first — children often already know these. Then 3s and 4s. Leave 6s, 7s, 8s, and 9s until last; these are the hardest and benefit most from the confidence built by mastering the easier tables first.
Use the commutative property. If your child knows 3×7=21, they also know 7×3=21. That halves the number of facts to learn. Make sure they understand this — it's a genuine shortcut, not a trick.

Sodafom's Times Tables Race and Mental Maths Sprint games are built specifically for MTC preparation. They present facts in random order (just like the real test), time the responses, and adapt difficulty based on which facts the child finds hardest. Ten minutes before school, three times a week, and most children are MTC-ready within a term.
